narrative: The model estimates an 86% chance that you will leave your job, and because the promotion decision relies on that risk, you are being denied promotion at this time. The strongest signal was your total career experience: at 6–10 years, you differ from the typical stay-predicted employee, about half of whom have only 1–5 years, so your longer track record makes a move more plausible. The second most influential factor was that you already have other job opportunities; most employees predicted to stay do not, which strongly pushed the prediction toward leaving. Third was your time in the current organization, at 1–5 years. Although this is common among stayers, in your overall profile it still pointed toward leaving, suggesting you are at a mobile point rather than a settled long-tenure stage. These signals are reinforced by low monthly pay relative to the stay group, no bonus, low support, no recognition, low emotional commitment, and low job satisfaction. Next, the organization should review your pay, recognition, support, and growth path, and discuss whether a clear promotion route could retain you. You should also clarify your intentions and weigh current opportunities against what the employer is prepared to change.
